data.pni_summary: What could happen if something goes wrong? As of January 14, 2021, Google officially became the owner of Fitbit. That worried many privacy conscious users. However, Google promised that “Fitbit users’ health and wellness data won't be used for Google ads and this data will be kept separate from other Google ad data” as part of the deal with global regulators when they bought Fitbit. This is good. And Fitbit seems to do an OK job with privacy and security. It de-identifies the data it collects so it's (hopefully) not personally identifiable. We say hopefully because, depending on the kind of data, it’s been found to be pretty easy to de-anonymize these data sets and track down an individual’s patterns, especially with location data. So, be aware with Fitbit—or any fitness tracker—you are strapping on a device that tracks your location, heart rate, sleep patterns, and more. That's a lot of personal information gathered in one place. What is not good is what can happen with all this very personal health data if others aren't careful. A recent report showed that health data for over 61 million fitness tracker users, including both Fitbit and Apple, was exposed when a third-party company that allowed users to sync their health data from their fitness trackers did not secure the data properly. Personal information such as names, birthdates, weight, height, gender, and geographical location for Fitbit and other fitness-tracker users was left exposed because the company didn't passwo

headline: Fitbit Tracks Your Life
verdict_md:
Fitbit's Charge 6 Premium Fitness Tracker collects a wide range of personal data, including your name, email address, password, date of birth, gender, height, weight, mobile telephone number, and profile photo. They also collect sensitive data such as biometrics, health information, and location data. This data is shared with corporate affiliates, service providers, third-party application developers, employers and insurance companies, and Google for joint processing of profile information. 
The scariest clause is the one that allows Fitbit to preserve or disclose information about you to comply with a law, regulation, legal process, or governmental request. 
Fitbit has a good track record with no reported breaches, but the fact that they use AI training with health data is a concern. 
Tips to protect yourself:
* Be cautious when sharing personal information, especially sensitive data like biometrics and health information.
* Review Fitbit's privacy policy and opt-out mechanisms to control how your data is shared.
* Consider using a pseudonym or limiting the amount of personal information you share on the platform.
